newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia gives 'final' war criminal list to Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Croatia gives 'final' war criminal list to Serbs.

text.p: The Croatian government, under pressure from the United Nations, has whittled its wanted list of Serb war crimes suspects down to 150 names, effectively promising other residents of Eastern Slavonia that they will not be prosecuted when Croatian rule is restored.
Suspects named on the list will be notified and U.N. administrators expect that those still in the enclave will flee before the Croatians take over.

Eastern Slavonia was one of three areas where local Serbs seized power in a 1991 revolt against Croatia's move to independence from Yugoslavia. It is now under temporary U.N. supervision and will revert to Croatian government rule with guarantees for minority rights following elections on April 13.

Officials said on Tuesday that Croatia's nationalist government came up with a list only under intense U.N. pressure and originally included more than 800 Serbs. It was cut to 175, then to 150 to defuse objections that it was too broad and open to misuse.

"UNTAES (U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia) has worked hard to create conditions necessary for ethnic Serbs to remain in Croatia in conditions of safety, security and dignity," the U.N. mission said in a statement.

"To reduce local anxiety and unjustified speculation and propaganda about war crimes, UNTAES has received from the government of Croatia a list of 150 persons who 1) have been convicted in absentia of crimes against international humanitarian law or 2) have been charged with one of these crimes or 3) are suspected of having committed one of (them)."
UNTAES spokesman Philip Arnold told Reuters that the mission had forwarded what was hoped to be the final list to Vojin Susa, the Serbs' secretary for justice issues.
Susa was asked to notify each person on the list and inform them of their legal rights, including due process and a defence attorney, to challenge the charges in court.

The "99.9 percent" of 120,000-odd Serb residents in Eastern Slavonia who do not receive a notification by March 25 "should consider themselves fully protected" by Croatia's war amnesty law enacted last year, Arnold said.
Arnold could not say who was on the list. Previous ones included some prominent hard-line nationalists.
Thousands of Serbs have departed Eastern Slavonia for Serbia in the run-up to the voting for municipal councils.
But UNTAES said the outflow had ebbed since late February with ever greater numbers of Serbs signing up to receive Croatian citizenship documents.
Arnold said more than 60,000 of the Serbs had obtained Croatian personal identity papers to date.

Diplomatic sources said federal Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro, was also prepared to approve dual citizenship for East Slavonian Serbs to encourage them to stay put after initially rejecting the idea outright.
"This may involve changing Yugoslav law but it will give much greater confidence to Serbs living here," one diplomat in the enclave said. "We understand this deal is very much on."
